narrative: Your promotion is denied because the model estimates an 86% probability that you will leave the organization. In practical terms, it sees your current situation as much closer to a departure pattern than a retention pattern, so a promotion is treated as a high-risk investment. The strongest influence was your overall experience of six to ten years. This is a relatively experienced profile—most employees predicted to stay have only one to five years overall—and it pushed the estimate toward leaving. The second strongest influence was that you have other job opportunities. This clearly pushed toward leaving and stands out because most employees predicted to stay reported no other opportunities. The third influence was your one-to-five years in this organization, which also pushed toward leaving, likely reflecting a stage when people reassess career progression. Together, these signals outweighed factors pointing toward staying. The organization should not rely on this prediction alone; it should discuss your career path, promotion timing, recognition, support, workload and pay, and whether other opportunities can be addressed through a retention plan. You should clarify what would make you stay and whether the promotion decision can be reconsidered with concrete commitments.
